html:
A road of about 1,000 km along the north of Java, from Anyer in the west to Panarukan in the east, built in 1808 to 1811 under the Dutch governor general Herman Willem Daendels with unpaid forced labour that cost thousands of lives.

Daendels was sent by the Kingdom of Holland, then ruled by Napoleon's brother Louis, to defend Java against the British. Ships were at risk from the Royal Navy, so he wanted a road to move troops and mail quickly along the island. Javanese rulers were ordered to supply workers, who cut through swamps, forests and mountain passes such as the one near Sumedang. Many died of disease, hunger and exhaustion. The road cut travel time across Java from weeks to days.

It did not save Dutch rule: the British took Java in 1811, and Stamford Raffles governed it until 1816. But the road became the spine of Java's transport, and much of it is still a main highway. Indonesians remember it as a symbol of colonial cruelty, notably in a book by Pramoedya Ananta Toer. See Dutch East Indies.
